title: GPU Infrastructure Zero to Hero
subtitle: From CPU versus GPU to an evidence-backed AI-infrastructure incident
intro: Understand GPU memory, work, telemetry, power, scheduling, and incidents through explicit calculations and replay. No GPU is needed to begin.
mode: Hardware-free arithmetic and synthetic telemetry replay

levels.title: Meet the CPU and GPU
levels.objective: Explain what parallel work is before installing or operating anything.

concepts.title: A CPU and GPU do different kinds of work
concepts.explanation:
A CPU is a general-purpose processor suited to many kinds of control and computation. A GPU provides substantial parallel processing capability for suitable workloads. Many AI operations use repeated arithmetic on arrays, which can benefit from GPU execution when the software and data flow are appropriate.

A GPU does not automatically make every program faster. Serial dependencies, small workloads, data transfer, memory capacity, and unsupported operations can limit benefits. The course begins with explicit teaching models; it does not pretend that your browser's animations are GPU benchmarks.
concepts.analogy: One versatile chef handles varied instructions; a coordinated team can prepare many similar tasks when the work can be divided.
concepts.example: Eight equal-cost independent tasks take eight rounds with one worker, or two idealized rounds with four workers. This is arithmetic reasoning, not a measured hardware speedup.
concepts.mistake: Parallel capacity cannot remove a dependency where the next step needs the previous result.

frames.narration: Start with equal-cost independent work.
The model assigns it to available workers.
Parallel workers handle independent tasks together.
The result illustrates a condition for parallel benefit, not a benchmark.

check.prompt: What is necessary for the simple four-worker model to finish tasks together?
options: Every task depends on the previous task
check.explanation: Parallel work must be divisible without violating dependencies.

concepts.title: A kernel, a workload, and a result
concepts.explanation:
A workload is the task and data being processed. A GPU kernel is code launched to perform an operation on the GPU. An application coordinates kernels, memory, input preparation, and output use. A hardware device, driver, runtime, and compatible libraries must all support the actual execution path.

A program requesting a GPU does not prove that useful GPU work occurred. Verify the execution path and measured result. This course's default calculator and replay require no GPU; the optional read-only collection script helps inspect compatible hardware later.
concepts.analogy: Owning a specialized machine and booking it is different from feeding it the right material and producing a verified result.
concepts.example: An AI inference application prepares input, runs model operations, and returns a prediction. Telemetry helps you see whether the GPU is used and what constrains it.
concepts.mistake: A container requesting a GPU is not evidence that the application launched a GPU kernel.

frames.narration: Preparation is part of the workload.
Supported code must actually execute on the GPU.
Output returns to the application.
Verify correctness and actual execution rather than only resource allocation.

check.prompt: Does reserving a GPU guarantee that a program used it?
options: No; verify the actual execution path
It proves there is no input bottleneck
check.explanation: Allocation and useful execution are separate outcomes.

concepts.title: The complete server still matters
concepts.explanation:
A GPU sits in a system with CPUs, host RAM, storage, network interfaces, power, and cooling. The CPU may prepare data; storage and networks deliver input; cooling and power enable sustained operation. A slow input path can leave a capable GPU waiting. A physical fault can interrupt an otherwise correct application.

Separate hardware-management evidence from workload telemetry. Redfish can expose supported platform-management information; DCGM provides NVIDIA GPU-related telemetry where supported. Neither source universally replaces the other, and availability depends on the actual system.
concepts.analogy: A fast kitchen still waits if ingredients arrive slowly or ventilation fails.
concepts.example: A low GPU utilization reading can coexist with high CPU input-preparation load. Investigate both before buying more GPUs.
concepts.mistake: Low utilization does not automatically mean the GPU is broken, and Redfish support does not guarantee every GPU workload metric is exposed.

frames.narration: Useful GPU work depends on the surrounding system.
Input delays can leave the GPU waiting.
Fixing input can change utilization.
Platform conditions can introduce a different constraint.

check.prompt: What can cause a capable GPU to wait?
options: A slow input or data-preparation path
check.explanation: The full pipeline supplies the GPU's work.

lab.goal: In the explicit equal-cost model, assign eight and twelve independent tasks to four workers and identify the GPU as the course's parallel-compute component.
hints: This exercise models independent tasks, not a hardware benchmark.
Use four workers and choose GPU; compare the number of idealized rounds.

questions.explanation: Allocation and useful execution are separate outcomes.

options: A slow input or data-preparation path

questions.explanation: A serial dependency still constrains the computation.

levels.title: VRAM, model weights, and precision
levels.objective: Calculate a weight footprint using explicit units and assumptions.

concepts.title: GPU memory is a capacity constraint
concepts.explanation:
VRAM is memory associated with a GPU. A workload needs space for data and intermediate state as well as model weights. Host RAM and GPU memory are distinct pools unless a particular system and runtime explicitly provide other behavior. A model can fail to fit even when the computer has ample host RAM.

Capacity is separate from current use. Report total memory and observed allocated or used memory with their actual definitions. A framework's reserved memory can differ from actively used data; a single number does not explain all allocation behavior.
concepts.analogy: The kitchen's workbench and the warehouse are separate spaces; abundant warehouse storage does not make the bench larger.
concepts.example: A 24 GiB GPU has a finite local budget. Model weights, per-request state, overhead, and other workloads compete for it.
concepts.mistake: Do not assume a server's 128 GiB host RAM means a 24 GiB GPU can hold 128 GiB of ordinary device allocations.

frames.narration: The system has different memory pools.
GPU-resident weights consume device capacity.
Additional workload state uses the remaining budget.
Check actual placement and capacity rather than adding unrelated pools.

check.prompt: Is host RAM automatically the same pool as ordinary GPU VRAM allocations?
options: Only when the disk is large
It always has the same total
No; placement and runtime behavior must be understood
check.explanation: Host and device memory have distinct placement and runtime semantics.

concepts.title: Parameters and bytes per parameter
concepts.explanation:
A model's parameter count and representation determine an approximate weight footprint. Multiply the number of parameters by bytes per stored parameter. FP32 commonly uses four bytes, FP16 two, and an illustrative INT8 representation one, before accounting for additional quantization metadata or other state.

Precision choices can affect accuracy, hardware support, and computation. A smaller storage representation is not a free guarantee of equivalent model quality. The calculator explicitly estimates weights, per-request allowance, overhead, and optionally optimizer allowance; it does not measure actual framework memory.
concepts.analogy: The number of books and the size of each book determine shelf space, but packaging can add overhead.
concepts.example: Seven billion parameters × two bytes = 14 billion bytes, approximately 13.04 GiB of FP16 weights. This is not the entire inference or training footprint.
concepts.mistake: Do not equate seven billion parameters with seven GiB, or assume weight memory is the complete allocation.

frames.narration: Parameter count alone is insufficient.
Changing storage bytes changes the estimated footprint.
The arithmetic compares weight storage only.
Accuracy, support, and total allocation remain separate checks.

check.prompt: What is the basic weight-footprint calculation?
options: Always one GiB per billion parameters
Parameter count × bytes per stored parameter
check.explanation: The estimate needs both count and representation size.

concepts.title: Bytes, MiB, and GiB
concepts.explanation:
Memory values need a scale. A byte contains eight bits. MiB equals 1,048,576 bytes, and GiB equals 1,073,741,824 bytes. Decimal GB uses one billion bytes. Convert explicitly when comparing a reported metric to an estimated model footprint.

Some GPU telemetry fields use MiB, while this calculator displays GiB. Preserve field definitions and display labels. A 14-billion-byte estimate is about 13.04 GiB, so a capacity decision near the limit can change if units are mixed or overhead is ignored.
concepts.analogy: A measurement in inches and one in centimeters need conversion before comparison.
concepts.example: 24,576 MiB equals 24 GiB. Divide MiB by 1024 for GiB. Divide bytes by 2^30 for GiB.
concepts.mistake: Relabeling MiB as GiB without conversion makes the capacity report wrong by a large factor.

frames.narration: The same capacity has different numeric representations.
Convert bytes to the intended scale.
Convert MiB to GiB explicitly.
Compare values only after their units agree.

check.prompt: How many GiB are 24,576 MiB?
check.explanation: 1024 MiB equals one GiB.

lab.goal: Choose FP16 so the supplied seven-billion-parameter and thirteen-billion-parameter weight plans fit their respective exercise memory budgets with stated overhead.
hints: The goal specifically asks for FP16; smaller formats have separate quality and support questions.
Choose FP16 and inspect weights, overhead, and per-request allowance.

questions.prompt: Is host RAM automatically the same pool as ordinary GPU VRAM allocations?
options: Only when the disk is large
It always has the same total
No; placement and runtime behavior must be understood
questions.explanation: Host and device memory have distinct placement and runtime semantics.

questions.prompt: What is the basic weight-footprint calculation?
options: Always one GiB per billion parameters
Parameter count × bytes per stored parameter
questions.explanation: The estimate needs both count and representation size.

questions.prompt: How many GiB are 24,576 MiB?
questions.explanation: 1024 MiB equals one GiB.

questions.prompt: Does the weight footprint include every training allocation?
options: No; gradients, optimizer state, activations, and other allocations may be additional
questions.explanation: Weights are one contribution to total memory.

questions.prompt: Does smaller precision guarantee unchanged model quality?
options: It proves every kernel is faster
No; validate quality and hardware/software support
questions.explanation: Storage savings and quality or speed are separate outcomes.

levels.title: Why a model can still run out of memory
levels.objective: Include request state, batching, overhead, and training-specific allocations.

concepts.title: Inference has more than weights
concepts.explanation:
Inference computes model outputs from inputs. Depending on the model and runtime, it needs activations, temporary workspace, input and output buffers, caches, and framework allocations. Some language-model workloads retain a key-value cache related to the generated or processed sequence. Its size depends on architecture, sequence lengths, precision, and batching.

The calculator uses an explicit per-request allowance instead of pretending one universal cache formula fits every model. Inspect the assumptions, then measure actual allocations on the intended runtime when moving beyond the teaching exercise.
concepts.analogy: A recipe book fits on the bench, but preparing meals also needs ingredients, utensils, and temporary space.
concepts.example: Estimated total = weights + batch × per-request allowance + overhead. A plan close to total VRAM leaves little room for differences from the assumptions.
concepts.mistake: A model's weight size alone does not establish that its maximum requested sequence length and concurrency will fit.

frames.narration: Weights consume only part of the memory.
The teaching plan declares other allowances explicitly.
Request count changes one contribution.
The arithmetic estimate prepares a measured runtime check.

check.prompt: Why can a model run out of memory even if its weights fit?
options: Other workload and runtime allocations also consume memory
Weights are always the entire workload
A trace ID takes all VRAM
Host RAM and GPU memory are automatically interchangeable
check.explanation: Weights, request state, workspace, and runtime allocations share the budget.

concepts.title: Batching trades memory and behavior
concepts.explanation:
A batch groups inputs for processing. Larger batches can change utilization and throughput while increasing memory requirements and potentially changing latency. The relationship depends on kernels, model, input sizes, and runtime. Do not assume a larger batch always improves every outcome.

Our capacity exercise chooses the largest batch that fits an explicit arithmetic model. It is not an optimizer for latency or production throughput. The transfer scenario changes VRAM capacity, so a reusable strategy recomputes the plan rather than hard-coding one batch number.
concepts.analogy: Cooking more meals together can use the stove efficiently while requiring more bench space and changing wait times.
concepts.example: With 7B FP16 weights, 2 GiB overhead, and 1 GiB per request, the model's largest batch is eight on 24 GiB and four on 20 GiB.
concepts.mistake: A batch that fits the estimate is not automatically the best latency choice or a guarantee against fragmentation and runtime overhead.

frames.narration: The first capacity allows a larger batch.
A smaller capacity changes the feasible plan.
A strategy recomputes from the new budget.
Memory fit and application performance remain separate objectives.

check.prompt: Should a batch number be hard-coded when capacity changes?
options: No; recompute from the relevant memory assumptions
Keep the same batch whenever parameter count is unchanged
check.explanation: Capacity and workload assumptions determine the feasible plan.

concepts.title: Training adds other state
concepts.explanation:
Training updates model parameters using computed gradients and an optimizer. It can retain activations for backward computation, gradients, optimizer state, and sometimes additional parameter representations. The memory footprint depends on the chosen training method, optimizer, precision, distribution strategy, and implementation.

The calculator's training switch adds an explicit bytes-per-parameter optimizer allowance. That is a teaching estimate, not a complete formula for every training framework. It helps explain why an inference-fitting model may not fit training on the same GPU.
concepts.analogy: Studying a finished document takes less workspace than editing it while retaining drafts and change notes.
concepts.example: Toggle the training estimate in the sandbox. The declared optimizer allowance adds memory even though the parameter count and stored weight precision stay unchanged.
concepts.mistake: Do not apply a single optimizer-byte constant as a universal total training-memory requirement.

frames.narration: Begin with the inference contributions.
Training introduces additional state.
The exact allocation depends on implementation choices.
Use the estimate to understand the budget before measuring reality.

check.prompt: Why might an inference-fitting model fail to fit training?
options: The GPU no longer uses bytes
Training can require gradients, optimizer state, and retained activations
check.explanation: Training introduces additional workload state.

lab.goal: Calculate the largest integer batch for BOTH scenarios: 24 GiB and 20 GiB capacity. Use 7 billion FP16 parameters, 2 GiB overhead, and 1 GiB per request. The estimate must fit; then explain why it is not a latency guarantee.
hints: Convert 7 billion × 2 bytes to GiB, then add 2 GiB overhead.
Divide the remaining capacity by the 1 GiB request allowance and round down to an integer.
The fixed footprint is about 15.04 GiB: batches eight and four fit the two capacities, while the next integers exceed them.

questions.prompt: Why can a model run out of memory even if its weights fit?
options: Other workload and runtime allocations also consume memory
Weights are always the entire workload
A trace ID takes all VRAM
Host RAM and GPU memory are automatically interchangeable
questions.explanation: Weights, request state, workspace, and runtime allocations share the budget.

questions.prompt: Should a batch number be hard-coded when capacity changes?
options: No; recompute from the relevant memory assumptions
Keep the same batch whenever parameter count is unchanged
questions.explanation: Capacity and workload assumptions determine the feasible plan.

questions.prompt: Why might an inference-fitting model fail to fit training?
options: The GPU no longer uses bytes
Training can require gradients, optimizer state, and retained activations
questions.explanation: Training introduces additional workload state.

questions.prompt: Does the largest memory-fitting batch necessarily give the best latency?
options: It proves all kernels are optimal
There is no latency in inference
No; measure the workload's latency and throughput objectives
questions.explanation: Fit and performance are different objectives.

questions.prompt: What should accompany a memory estimate?
options: Its assumptions and subsequent runtime measurements
Only the total parameter count without memory assumptions
questions.explanation: Explicit assumptions make an estimate reviewable and comparable with reality.

levels.title: Read GPU telemetry
levels.objective: Preserve metric meaning, units, availability, and observation time.

concepts.title: DCGM and its exporter
concepts.explanation:
NVIDIA DCGM provides tools and interfaces for observing and managing supported NVIDIA data-center GPU environments. DCGM Exporter exposes selected telemetry fields in Prometheus format. Actual field availability depends on hardware, driver, DCGM version, permissions, and configuration. A configured field is not a guarantee that every system emits it.

The default course supplies synthetic, labeled metric fixtures. Optional collection uses an existing compatible local tool in read-only mode. Installing the exporter alone does not establish useful metrics, correct scrape configuration, or a healthy GPU.
concepts.analogy: A measuring instrument and its reporting adapter are useful only for measurements the equipment actually supports.
concepts.example: The replay emits example temperature, power, memory, utilization, and error-code fields. It marks every sample as synthetic teaching data.
concepts.mistake: Missing telemetry is not a zero measurement. Confirm support and runtime output before defining an alert.

frames.narration: Telemetry starts with a supported environment.
Selected available fields become samples.
Unavailable fields need explicit handling.
Verify actual runtime output before building queries.

check.prompt: Does selecting a DCGM field guarantee it appears on every GPU?
options: No; availability depends on the runtime environment
check.explanation: Hardware, driver, permissions, and configuration affect emission.

concepts.title: Memory used and total need compatible units
concepts.explanation:
A memory-used reading and a total-capacity reading can support a utilization fraction when they describe the same device and compatible quantities. Match the GPU identity and unit. GPU telemetry may describe framebuffer memory rather than a framework's exact live-tensor allocation. Interpret the source definition.

Our replay reports used and total memory in MiB. Dividing used by total produces a fraction; multiplying by 100 produces a percentage. An absent or zero denominator needs explicit handling rather than a fabricated healthy ratio.
concepts.analogy: Occupied seats divided by total seats gives occupancy only if both counts refer to the same theater.
concepts.example: 12,000 MiB / 24,576 MiB × 100 is about 48.8%. Keep the gpu label when comparing readings.
concepts.mistake: Do not divide one device's used memory by another device's total, or divide MiB by unconverted GiB.

frames.narration: Match the same device.
Identify numerator and denominator.
Confirm unit compatibility and valid capacity.
The resulting percentage has a defined meaning.

check.prompt: What must agree before computing a used/total GPU-memory fraction?
check.explanation: The fraction requires matching quantities on the same resource.

concepts.title: A sample is an observation, not a diagnosis
concepts.explanation:
A metric sample has a value and identity at a relevant observation time. Temperature, power, memory, and utilization describe different quantities. Compare trends and related fields to form a hypothesis, and keep collection failures distinct from hardware failures. An exporter can stop while the GPU continues running.

The replay contains known teaching scenarios so you can practice interpretation. Its thresholds are disclosed scenario rules, not universal manufacturer limits. In real operation, consult field semantics and the equipment's actual requirements.
concepts.analogy: A photograph records one view; several time-stamped views and related measurements support a story.
concepts.example: Rising used memory approaching total capacity supports a memory-pressure investigation. It does not by itself prove a particular framework allocation failed.
concepts.mistake: Do not substitute a missing exporter response with zero utilization and conclude that the application stopped.

frames.narration: One observation has limited scope.
A trend adds time context.
Related fields refine the explanation.
Collection quality and application evidence remain part of the diagnosis.

check.prompt: An exporter is unreachable. What can you conclude about GPU utilization?
options: Its utilization evidence is unavailable from that scrape
check.explanation: Collection failure does not establish the underlying hardware state.

lab.goal: Select the example GPU framebuffer-used metric and its MiB unit. Inspect its matching total-memory sample and calculated percentage.
hints: Use the sample's field meaning and unit rather than its numeric size.
Choose DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED and MiB for this fixture.

options: No; availability depends on the runtime environment
questions.explanation: Hardware, driver, permissions, and configuration affect emission.

questions.explanation: The fraction requires matching quantities on the same resource.

questions.prompt: An exporter is unreachable. What can you conclude about GPU utilization?

questions.prompt: A field is missing. How should it be represented?
options: Unavailable or unknown with collection context
questions.explanation: Missing evidence must remain distinct from a measured zero.

levels.title: Utilization, throughput, and latency
levels.objective: Distinguish busy hardware from useful application results.

concepts.title: Utilization is not success
concepts.explanation:
A GPU-utilization reading describes activity according to the field's sampling definition. It is not model accuracy, request success, throughput, or an exact universal efficiency score. A busy GPU can do wasteful work, and a lightly used GPU can be appropriate for a small workload.

Read application outcomes alongside hardware observations. Compare the measurement window and actual field semantics. The replay demonstrates plausible patterns but cannot benchmark your model or prove that one utilization target is best for every application.
concepts.analogy: A busy kitchen is not automatically serving correct meals quickly.
concepts.example: Compare utilization with completed requests, error evidence, and latency. A rise in activity without useful output is not automatically an improvement.
concepts.mistake: Do not equate 100% utilization with perfect efficiency or healthy service.

frames.narration: Activity is one observation.
Measure useful output separately.
Busy hardware can coexist with a poor result.
Choose an application objective before optimizing.

check.prompt: Does 100% utilization guarantee good application results?
options: No; success, throughput, and latency are separate
It proves every model is accurate
check.explanation: Hardware activity is not an application outcome.

concepts.title: Find an input-starved GPU
concepts.explanation:
A workload can wait for storage reads, network transfer, CPU preparation, tokenization, or a queue feeding the GPU. Low GPU activity with low power and slow useful output can support an input-starvation hypothesis. Additional evidence should identify the actual waiting stage.

Our replay explicitly models an input-starved case, and the lab asks you to inspect the input path rather than assume a GPU defect. Real profiling, CPU metrics, application traces, and queue measurements add evidence beyond these synthetic fields.
concepts.analogy: A chef can wait idle when ingredients are not prepared, even if the stove works.
concepts.example: The training case has 15% utilization, 65 W power, and a slower request-counter increase. Its appropriate next investigation is the input pipeline.
concepts.mistake: Adding GPUs can add idle capacity when the bottleneck remains upstream.

frames.narration: Upstream work supplies the GPU.
The replay shows an explicit waiting pattern.
Investigate the upstream stage with additional evidence.
Verify output after an appropriate change.

check.prompt: What is an appropriate next investigation for the modeled input-starved case?
check.explanation: The synthetic pattern points to work arriving too slowly.

concepts.title: Measure throughput and latency separately
concepts.explanation:
Throughput is completed useful work per time interval. Latency is elapsed time for a defined operation. Batching, concurrency, queues, and workload sizes can affect them differently. A change that increases total completed requests can also increase some users' waiting time.

The replay provides a cumulative request counter and timestamps. Compute throughput from its change over an interval while considering reset semantics. This synthetic counter is an application metric, not a DCGM field. A real latency distribution requires actual request-duration observations.
concepts.analogy: A bus carries more passengers per trip but may make one passenger wait longer than a taxi.
concepts.example: A training counter rising from 100 to 340 over 60 seconds represents four modeled requests per second in a reset-free interval.
concepts.mistake: The last counter value is not a rate, and an application request metric should not be mistaken for GPU hardware telemetry.

frames.narration: Begin with a cumulative count and observation time.
Compute change over a meaningful interval.
The same rate can appear in another comparable interval.
Request latency requires separate measurements.

check.prompt: What is throughput for 240 additional requests over 60 seconds without resets?
check.explanation: Throughput divides useful-count change by elapsed time.

lab.goal: Inspect the healthy and input-starved replays. Select the next investigation appropriate to slow input delivery instead of assuming a GPU defect.
hints: Low utilization with low power can mean the device is waiting for work.
Choose inspect_input_pipeline and inspect the workload-counter trend.

options: No; success, throughput, and latency are separate

questions.explanation: Hardware activity is not an application outcome.

questions.explanation: The synthetic pattern points to work arriving too slowly.

questions.explanation: Throughput divides useful-count change by elapsed time.

levels.title: Power, heat, and clock changes
levels.objective: Interpret a thermal pattern using related readings and actual equipment limits.

concepts.title: Power and energy
concepts.explanation:
Power describes the rate of energy use and is commonly measured in watts. Energy accumulates consumption over time, such as joules or watt-hours. A current power sample does not alone determine total energy consumption across a workload. You need time and the relevant interval or accumulated energy measurement.

Power limits and supported controls are hardware-specific. The teaching app does not change device settings. Observe the field meaning and workload outcome before forming a tuning hypothesis, and use actual equipment procedures for real interventions.
concepts.analogy: Water flow per second differs from the total water collected in a tank.
concepts.example: A steady 200 W for one hour corresponds to 200 Wh under that constant-power assumption. A varying workload requires integration or an appropriate energy counter.
concepts.mistake: Do not interpret a watt reading as cumulative energy or increase a limit simply because throughput is low.

frames.narration: A power sample describes a rate.
Time turns a constant rate into an energy estimate.
The interval changes the accumulated quantity.
Varying power requires appropriate accumulation.

check.prompt: Is a 200 W sample already a 200 Wh energy total?
options: No; energy also depends on time and variation
check.explanation: Power and energy are different quantities.

concepts.title: Temperature and clock behavior
concepts.explanation:
A GPU can adjust operating clocks for several reasons, including workload demand, power constraints, thermal constraints, and configured behavior. A clock decrease alongside rising temperature supports a thermal hypothesis in our explicit replay. It is not a universal diagnosis from two numbers alone.

Use supported limit and reason fields when available, equipment specifications, workload measurements, and system cooling evidence. The replay's 85 °C decision threshold is a teaching rule, not a safe operating limit for all GPUs.
concepts.analogy: A runner may slow because of heat, terrain, pacing, or another constraint; speed alone does not explain the reason.
concepts.example: The thermal fixture warms from 55 °C toward 91 °C while its later clock falls from 1500 to 900 MHz and modeled throughput declines.
concepts.mistake: Do not treat every lower clock as thermal throttling or use this course's threshold as a manufacturer specification.

frames.narration: Start with related baseline observations.
The modeled temperature rises.
Later clock and output changes support the teaching hypothesis.
Real diagnosis needs hardware limits and additional evidence.

check.prompt: Does a lower GPU clock always prove thermal throttling?
options: It is always a driver bug
No; several constraints or workload states can change clocks
check.explanation: Clock behavior needs context and supporting evidence.

concepts.title: Cooling belongs to the physical system
concepts.explanation:
Cooling conditions involve the GPU, server airflow, fans, chassis, rack environment, and potentially facility systems. A supported management interface can provide related platform observations. An application metric may reveal the user impact. Connect these layers using equipment identity and timing.

The lab asks for a cooling investigation rather than an automatic real repair. A technician follows equipment procedures, then the operator verifies temperature, clocks, health, and application outcomes. Physical maintenance and firmware configuration are not interchangeable responses.
concepts.analogy: A hot kitchen can depend on building ventilation, not merely the chef's recipe.
concepts.example: Inspect the thermal replay, compare system fan and inlet evidence where available, and plan maintenance appropriate to the actual equipment.
concepts.mistake: Raising a power limit cannot be assumed to fix cooling and can change the system's operating constraints.

frames.narration: The device observation begins the investigation.
Platform evidence helps explain the condition.
Any real response follows equipment procedures.
Verification spans hardware and application outcomes.

check.prompt: What is a sensible response to the course's thermal replay?
options: Investigate cooling with related evidence and actual equipment limits
check.explanation: The response should address the suspected physical constraint.

lab.goal: Compare the healthy and thermal replays. Choose a cooling investigation, preserving temperature, clock, and workload evidence.
hints: A teaching threshold is not a universal GPU operating limit.
Choose inspect_cooling and compare the related temperature, clock, and request readings.

options: No; energy also depends on time and variation
questions.explanation: Power and energy are different quantities.

questions.prompt: Does a lower GPU clock always prove thermal throttling?
options: It is always a driver bug
No; several constraints or workload states can change clocks
questions.explanation: Clock behavior needs context and supporting evidence.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible response to the course's thermal replay?
options: Investigate cooling with related evidence and actual equipment limits
questions.explanation: The response should address the suspected physical constraint.

questions.prompt: Which scope should be stated for the 85 °C rule?
options: It is the disclosed teaching-scenario threshold
It is every GPU's safe limit
It proves every fan is broken

questions.prompt: What should verify a real cooling response?
options: Relevant hardware readings and application outcomes afterward
questions.explanation: Recovery requires evidence of the intended condition and useful result.

levels.title: GPU errors and evidence preservation
levels.objective: Distinguish an error code, an error count, and an appropriate investigation.

concepts.title: An XID value is an error identifier
concepts.explanation:
NVIDIA error identifiers can indicate classes of GPU-related errors, but interpretation depends on the documented identifier and surrounding evidence. A field containing the latest error code is not a cumulative count of error events. Applying a rate function to a numeric code does not produce a meaningful error-event rate.

The replay uses a nonzero illustrative code to trigger its teaching scenario. It does not diagnose a real device from that value alone. Consult the manufacturer's error guidance, driver logs, workload state, and hardware health when interpreting actual failures.
concepts.analogy: A hospital's case category number is not a count of patients.
concepts.example: The fixture changes xid_code from zero to a nonzero identifier. The lesson is to preserve the identifier and related event evidence, not divide the code by elapsed time.
concepts.mistake: Do not confuse a latest-code gauge with an exporter-owned event counter or infer one universal repair from an identifier.

frames.narration: The fixture initially has no injected error.
A numeric identifier appears.
Its persistence does not make it a cumulative count.
Preserve its meaning and inspect supporting evidence.

check.prompt: Can rate(latest_error_code) represent a meaningful error-event rate?
options: Yes, if the identifier persists across multiple samples
It is always requests per second
No; an identifier is not a cumulative event count
check.explanation: Numeric codes and cumulative counters have different semantics.

concepts.title: ECC and other health evidence
concepts.explanation:
Error-correcting memory mechanisms can detect and in some cases correct certain memory errors on supported equipment. Correctable and uncorrectable observations have different meanings and require their documented definitions. Availability, reset behavior, scope, and event history matter when interpreting counts or states.

A single field does not establish every fault's cause or severity. Combine health evidence with driver events, workload failures, device identity, and time. The course's basic replay does not implement ECC hardware, stress testing, or native diagnostic tools.
concepts.analogy: A spell-check correction differs from an unreadable page; both require knowing what was observed.
concepts.example: If a supported diagnostic reports an uncorrectable memory error, preserve its device identity and logs and follow the equipment's operational procedure.
concepts.mistake: Do not treat every error-related number as interchangeable, or assume absent ECC telemetry proves no errors occurred.

frames.narration: Begin with the actual field definition.
Keep the device and time context.
Different error classes can require different responses.
A decision follows documented evidence rather than a unitless number.

check.prompt: Is missing ECC telemetry proof that no memory error occurred?
options: It is a successful stress test
No; support and evidence availability must be checked
It proves the GPU is new
check.explanation: Unavailable evidence is not a verified absence of failures.

concepts.title: Isolation and evidence before disruption
concepts.explanation:
When a device is suspected of causing failures, operations may involve limiting new work, preserving logs, checking health, and following a maintenance procedure. The specific response depends on the failure and the platform. A blind reset can disrupt jobs and erase transient evidence without addressing the cause.

The teaching policy chooses isolation and evidence collection for the injected GPU-error case. It performs no actual quarantine or reset. Read-only collection and a documented decision are the first transferable skills; real intervention needs hardware-specific procedures and authorization.
concepts.analogy: Close the suspect workbench to new tasks and record what happened before dismantling it.
concepts.example: Retain the replay's device, error identifier, clock, utilization, and application-counter history. State what additional driver and workload evidence you would collect.
concepts.mistake: Resetting first and investigating later can lose evidence and repeat the failure.

frames.narration: Identify the affected resource precisely.
Preserve observations and avoid adding risky work.
Investigate with the platform's procedures.
Any return to service needs verification.

check.prompt: What fits the injected GPU-error scenario better than a blind reset?
options: Isolate the suspected resource and collect evidence
check.explanation: Preserve evidence and choose an equipment-specific response.

lab.goal: Compare healthy and GPU-error replay evidence. Select an investigation that preserves the identifier and workload history without blindly resetting equipment.
hints: A code is an identifier, not an event count.
Choose isolate_and_collect_evidence; inspect the device and timestamped history.

questions.prompt: Can rate(latest_error_code) represent a meaningful error-event rate?
options: Yes, if the identifier persists across multiple samples
It is always requests per second
No; an identifier is not a cumulative event count
questions.explanation: Numeric codes and cumulative counters have different semantics.

questions.prompt: Is missing ECC telemetry proof that no memory error occurred?
options: It is a successful stress test
No; support and evidence availability must be checked
It proves the GPU is new
questions.explanation: Unavailable evidence is not a verified absence of failures.

questions.prompt: What fits the injected GPU-error scenario better than a blind reset?
options: Isolate the suspected resource and collect evidence
questions.explanation: Preserve evidence and choose an equipment-specific response.

questions.prompt: Why preserve driver and workload evidence before a disruptive operation?
options: It can explain the condition and prevent evidence loss
questions.explanation: Evidence supports a targeted, reviewable maintenance decision.

questions.prompt: Does this replay validate ECC or native GPU diagnostics?
options: It runs a physical memory stress test
No; it teaches explicitly bounded evidence interpretation
questions.explanation: The replay is not hardware qualification.

levels.title: Multiple GPUs and communication
levels.objective: Separate replication, sharding, memory placement, and interconnect constraints.

concepts.title: Data parallelism replicates work state
concepts.explanation:
Data parallelism distributes different data items across replicas of a computation. A common training design gives each worker a model replica and synchronizes relevant updates. Replication can improve processing capacity for suitable workloads, but each replica still needs its own required model state.

Simply adding two devices does not always combine their memory into one transparent allocation. Placement and framework behavior must be configured. The teaching calculator compares weight placement only, without running distributed computation or predicting actual speed.
concepts.analogy: Two kitchens with the same recipe each need their own recipe book and equipment.
concepts.example: A 13.04 GiB weight replica does not fit into each 10 GiB GPU just because two such GPUs exist.
concepts.mistake: Adding the VRAM labels of separate devices does not establish a usable contiguous budget for an unchanged workload.

frames.narration: Each device has its own capacity.
Replication repeats the weight requirement.
Total capacity across devices is not automatic placement.
Choose and validate a supported distribution strategy.

check.prompt: Does ordinary replication split a model's weight footprint across devices?
options: It automatically forms one memory pool
No; replicas can each need the full weights
check.explanation: Replication and sharding are different placement strategies.

concepts.title: Model parallelism partitions state or work
concepts.explanation:
Model-parallel designs divide parts of a model or its computation across devices. Tensor and pipeline parallelism are examples with different partition and communication behavior. A framework must implement the chosen strategy; merely requesting several GPUs does not configure it.

Our idealized exercise divides FP16 weights evenly across devices and adds a stated per-device overhead. It tests capacity arithmetic, not real tensor partitions, activation sizes, collective behavior, or numerical correctness. Actual distribution requires implementation and measurement.
concepts.analogy: A large production line can divide stages or tasks across workbenches rather than copying the entire line on every bench.
concepts.example: 13.04 GiB weights evenly divided across two GPUs is about 6.52 GiB each; adding 2 GiB assumed overhead fits the 10 GiB teaching capacity.
concepts.mistake: Even-sharding arithmetic is not a guarantee that the framework can make that partition or that the whole workload fits.

frames.narration: Start with the full weight footprint.
The model divides it under an explicit assumption.
Add the per-device allowance.
The arithmetic result prepares actual framework validation.

check.prompt: What additional requirement follows a sharding memory estimate?
options: Every GPU's memory is automatically shared
A supported framework partition and measured runtime validation
Only increasing the GPU resource count in the Pod
check.explanation: Placement arithmetic and executable distribution are different evidence.

concepts.title: Interconnects can determine the tradeoff
concepts.explanation:
Distributed computation exchanges data through supported device and network paths. PCIe, supported NVLink arrangements, host networks, and topology can affect available communication. Collective operations synchronize or combine work across participants, and communication can limit the benefit of adding workers.

Topology and supported links vary by hardware. Do not infer connectivity from the number of GPUs alone. Inspect actual devices and paths, use appropriate libraries, and measure the workload. The course illustrates communication but does not run or benchmark collectives.
concepts.analogy: Two workshops can cooperate, but the time to move materials between them can dominate the work.
concepts.example: A model partition may fit memory while spending substantial time moving intermediate data. Capacity success and throughput success remain separate.
concepts.mistake: More GPUs can add communication overhead; a supported interconnect name alone does not guarantee a speedup.

frames.narration: Partitioned work can create communication dependencies.
Moving data adds cost.
Synchronization affects elapsed completion time.
Measure the actual topology and workload rather than assuming linear scaling.

check.prompt: Can a model fit across GPUs but still scale poorly?
options: Yes; communication and synchronization can limit useful speedup
check.explanation: Capacity and distributed performance have different constraints.

lab.goal: Choose model partitioning rather than full replication for the supplied 7B FP16 weight footprint. Validate the idealized per-device budget on two different GPU layouts.
hints: Each data-parallel replica still needs its full weights.
Choose model and inspect weights plus overhead per GPU; this is a capacity estimate only.

questions.prompt: Does ordinary replication split a model's weight footprint across devices?
options: It automatically forms one memory pool
No; replicas can each need the full weights
questions.explanation: Replication and sharding are different placement strategies.

questions.prompt: What additional requirement follows a sharding memory estimate?
options: Every GPU's memory is automatically shared
A supported framework partition and measured runtime validation
Only increasing the GPU resource count in the Pod
questions.explanation: Placement arithmetic and executable distribution are different evidence.

questions.prompt: Can a model fit across GPUs but still scale poorly?
options: Yes; communication and synchronization can limit useful speedup
questions.explanation: Capacity and distributed performance have different constraints.

questions.prompt: Does requesting multiple GPUs configure tensor parallelism by itself?
options: No; the workload and framework must implement it
questions.explanation: Resource allocation and computation placement are separate.

questions.prompt: What should a scaling claim include?
options: Actual workload measurements and topology context
Only the theoretical sum of VRAM
Only the total parameter count without memory assumptions
questions.explanation: Scaling requires evidence beyond device quantity.

levels.title: GPU scheduling and isolation
levels.objective: Read a whole-GPU Pod request and reason about capacity and pending jobs.

concepts.title: Nodes, Pods, and the scheduler
concepts.explanation:
A Kubernetes node provides compute resources. A Pod groups containers scheduled onto a node. The scheduler places work according to declared resources and other constraints. GPU resources require supported drivers and a configured device-plugin or equivalent supported integration. A Pod requesting a GPU still needs compatible application software to use it.

Our first-fit scheduler is a teaching model using whole-GPU counts. It is not the Kubernetes scheduler and omits CPU, memory, affinity, topology, priorities, and many operational constraints. The optional Pod example illustrates resource declarations only.
concepts.analogy: A booking system assigns rooms based on available capacity and requested requirements.
concepts.example: Three one-GPU jobs fit capacities of two plus one in the first model. With only two total eligible GPUs, one job remains Pending.
concepts.mistake: A Pending job does not automatically indicate a broken GPU; capacity or other constraints may prevent placement.

frames.narration: The first layout has enough whole-GPU capacity.
The teaching model places three jobs.
The transfer layout has less capacity.
An unplaced job remains pending rather than sharing automatically.

check.prompt: A job remains Pending in the capacity model. What can that mean?
options: Its request is a metric sample
check.explanation: Pending placement and hardware health are different conditions.

concepts.title: Whole-GPU resource declarations
concepts.explanation:
A conventional NVIDIA whole-GPU resource uses a named extended resource such as nvidia.com/gpu. In the documented limits-based pattern, GPU limits can imply requests; when both are explicitly specified they must match. Whole-GPU counts are not arbitrary fractions in this teaching model.

The YAML exercise declares one GPU for a container. Its image prints a message and does not run GPU computation. The validator checks the teaching subset; real admission and scheduling apply additional rules and require the configured GPU integration.
concepts.analogy: Reserve one complete workbench using the resource name the booking system recognizes.
concepts.example: `resources: {limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 1}}` declares a one-GPU limit in the example. The scheduler model applies that count to its node capacities.
concepts.mistake: Declaring 0.5 of the whole-GPU resource is not how this model configures sharing or MIG.

frames.narration: Declare the workload's requested resource.
Use the supported resource identity and count.
The teaching validator and scheduler inspect it.
Actual admission and execution need their own runtime setup.

check.prompt: Does nvidia.com/gpu: 0.5 enable sharing in this whole-GPU model?
options: No; use the supported resource model and integration
check.explanation: Whole-GPU allocation is different from configured sharing mechanisms.

concepts.title: MIG and sharing are different designs
concepts.explanation:
Supported Multi-Instance GPU configurations partition particular GPUs into hardware-defined instances with specified profiles. Other sharing arrangements have different isolation, resource, and scheduling behavior. Availability depends on hardware and configuration; a conceptual diagram cannot create instances on unsupported equipment.

The default course illustrates these distinctions but does not reconfigure MIG, install device plugins, or test isolation. Real multi-tenant operation requires understanding supported profiles, resource names, ownership, performance behavior, and relevant security boundaries.
concepts.analogy: Dividing a building into separately equipped rooms differs from letting several people take turns at one workbench.
concepts.example: A supported MIG profile can expose a distinct schedulable resource under a configured integration. That is different from requesting a fractional value of an ordinary whole-GPU resource.
concepts.mistake: Do not claim that all GPU models support MIG or that every sharing mode provides the same isolation.

frames.narration: These are distinct resource arrangements.
Partition profiles require supported hardware and configuration.
Scheduling and isolation semantics differ.
Validate the actual arrangement before making a multi-tenant claim.

check.prompt: Do all sharing modes provide identical isolation and GPU support?
options: No; validate the supported mechanism and hardware
A fractional YAML number creates hardware partitions
check.explanation: Sharing and hardware partitioning have distinct support and boundaries.

lab.goal: Write a one-GPU Pod declaration. Verify placement with three slots, then inspect the pending job when only two slots are available.

Change the GPU limit to integer 1; inspect both placement scenarios.

options: No; use the supported resource model and integration
questions.explanation: Whole-GPU allocation is different from configured sharing mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Do all sharing modes provide identical isolation and GPU support?
options: No; validate the supported mechanism and hardware
A fractional YAML number creates hardware partitions
questions.explanation: Sharing and hardware partitioning have distinct support and boundaries.

options: No; actual execution must be checked
questions.explanation: Scheduling and application execution are separate evidence.

options: Additional resource, affinity, topology, and policy constraints
questions.explanation: The teaching scheduler deliberately covers a bounded subset.

levels.title: Prometheus metrics and trustworthy alerts
levels.objective: Interpret exported fields correctly and connect them to your query skills.

concepts.title: Exposition, scraping, and querying
concepts.explanation:
Prometheus exposition is a representation of named samples with labels and numeric values. A scrape obtains a snapshot from an endpoint. A backend stores observations over time, and queries interpret that stored series. Exposing an endpoint does not prove that a scraper is configured or healthy.

Our fixture server exposes labeled synthetic GPU fields and an application counter. The default course parser reads a bounded numeric subset and does not implement PromQL. The optional Prometheus setup provides actual scraping; your PromQL course supplies the query language.
concepts.analogy: Publishing a scoreboard, recording it over time, and asking questions of the history are separate steps.
concepts.example: The example `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP{gpu="0"} 55` is one labeled sample. A successful scrape and stored history are needed for later trend queries.
concepts.mistake: A sample parser is not a time-series database or a full PromQL engine.

frames.narration: The endpoint provides a current representation.
A configured scraper requests it.
Storage adds observations over time.
A query operates on the stored history and semantics.

check.prompt: Does exposing /metrics alone establish stored queryable history?
options: It creates a trace for every sample
No; scraping and storage must also work
check.explanation: Exposition, collection, and storage are separate stages.

concepts.title: Codes, gauges, counters, and labels
concepts.explanation:
A gauge-like observation such as current temperature or latest error identifier differs from a cumulative count. Reset-aware rates belong to appropriate cumulative counters, not arbitrary numeric codes. Labels identify the observed resource and dimensions; grouping must preserve the question's meaning.

In this fixture, training_requests_total is an application counter and DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS is treated as a latest-code observation. Actual exporter versions and selected fields must be checked against their definitions; similarly named exporter-owned counters can have different semantics.
concepts.analogy: A category number is not a total, and a thermometer is not a turnstile.
concepts.example: Rate idea: `rate(training_requests_total[1m])`. Error-code investigation: inspect a nonzero latest code and its associated events, not rate(code).
concepts.mistake: A metric's familiar name is insufficient; inspect source semantics, configured type, unit, and actual emission.

frames.narration: Different numeric fields have different meanings.
Their changes are not interchangeable.
Choose a query appropriate to the underlying quantity.
Keep units and identity intact during interpretation.

check.prompt: Which fixture field supports a request-rate calculation?
check.explanation: Rates of events need a suitable cumulative quantity.

concepts.title: Alerts include collection quality
concepts.explanation:
An alert rule should express a meaningful condition over the right resource and time window. Consider transient observations, workload expectations, missing telemetry, and maintenance state. Separate a collection outage from a measured hardware fault. Thresholds need equipment and operational context.

The fixture's thermal and memory thresholds illustrate reasoning; they are not production recommendations. A real alert should include actionable context and a verification path. Connect quantitative symptoms to logs or traces when diagnosing workload impact, and to hardware management where supported.
concepts.analogy: A warning system needs both a smoke condition and a way to report when its own detector is disconnected.
concepts.example: An exporter-down condition says collection failed. A supported high-temperature condition says a sensor observed a defined value. They are different investigations.
concepts.mistake: Treating absent samples as zero can suppress an incident exactly when observation is unavailable.

frames.narration: Known healthy collection supports interpretation.
A measured condition triggers its own investigation.
Missing data triggers a different investigation.
Verification checks the relevant layer.

check.prompt: An exporter-down alert directly establishes what?
check.explanation: Collection evidence and underlying resource condition differ.

lab.goal: Read the exposition and correctly classify the latest XID value and application request total before choosing any rate expression.
hints: The type and underlying quantity must agree.
Treat XID as a latest identifier and training_requests_total as a cumulative application counter.

questions.prompt: Does exposing /metrics alone establish stored queryable history?
options: It creates a trace for every sample
No; scraping and storage must also work
questions.explanation: Exposition, collection, and storage are separate stages.

questions.prompt: Which fixture field supports a request-rate calculation?
questions.explanation: Rates of events need a suitable cumulative quantity.

questions.prompt: An exporter-down alert directly establishes what?
questions.explanation: Collection evidence and underlying resource condition differ.

questions.prompt: Should absent GPU samples be silently replaced with zero in an alert?
options: No; preserve and alert on unavailable evidence appropriately
questions.explanation: Unknown and measured-zero conditions have different meanings.

questions.prompt: Where can SPL or trace evidence help a GPU incident?
options: Turning every log into a gauge
Investigating related events and application symptoms
questions.explanation: Logs, traces, metrics, and hardware management provide complementary evidence.

levels.title: An AI-infrastructure incident
levels.objective: Choose a response for memory pressure versus thermal pressure and verify the modeled outcome.

concepts.title: Classify the pressure from evidence
concepts.explanation:
Memory pressure, thermal constraints, input starvation, and device errors can produce different evidence and need different investigations. Start with the symptom, resource identity, and time window. Compare related hardware and application signals, keeping unavailable information explicit. Avoid assuming that every slow request is a GPU fault.

The capstone supplies one memory-pressure replay and one thermal replay. Its disclosed classifier is a teaching rule. A real diagnosis requires application errors, driver and device evidence, supported limits, and alternate hypotheses.
concepts.analogy: A restaurant can be limited by workspace, ventilation, ingredient delivery, or equipment failure; the response depends on which constraint is supported.
concepts.example: Memory near capacity supports a batch/allocation investigation. Rising temperature with clock reduction supports a cooling investigation in these explicit fixtures.
concepts.mistake: A universal restart policy does not address these different constraints and can disrupt work.

frames.narration: The two scenarios provide different pressure evidence.
Use related measurements to distinguish them.
Choose responses appropriate to their layers.
Verification is required for both branches.

check.prompt: Should memory pressure and thermal pressure always use the same response?
options: No; choose a response supported by the affected constraint
check.explanation: Different conditions require different evidence and interventions.

concepts.title: A response includes verification
concepts.explanation:
An allocation response can involve changes such as batching or concurrency, but it must preserve correctness and measure actual use. A cooling response belongs to equipment and environment investigation and maintenance. Both should preserve the initial evidence and verify useful workload outcomes, not just change a dashboard.

The capstone switches to a healthy synthetic replay after a correct modeled decision. That illustrates the verification workflow; it does not measure a physical repair or tune a real model. State this scope in the report and identify the real measurements you would collect next.
concepts.analogy: Moving furniture or repairing ventilation is useful only if the room becomes usable and its purpose still works.
concepts.example: Compare before and after memory, temperature, clock, and request-counter trends. Record the selected branch and what actual hardware or application testing remains.
concepts.mistake: The simulator's healthy after-state is not evidence that the same action universally repairs real equipment.

frames.narration: Record the initial condition.
Select a response for the supported hypothesis.
Inspect the new modeled evidence.
Explain the result and the real-world verification still required.

check.prompt: What should accompany a claimed improvement?
check.explanation: A claim needs an outcome measurement and honest boundaries.

concepts.title: Your three-course operational picture
concepts.explanation:
A server-management course explains physical resources and supported management actions. A telemetry course explains how applications emit connected evidence. A GPU course explains device capacity, workload behavior, and related operational constraints. Together they help you ask better questions across infrastructure layers.

Completing these labs establishes beginner-to-advanced conceptual and bounded practical objectives. Real operational expertise grows through varied applications, supported hardware, deployed collection pipelines, and supervised maintenance. A badge should encourage that next practice rather than conceal what has not been tested.
concepts.analogy: A useful engineer connects the building, the workers, and the records of their work.
concepts.example: Use Redfish for supported platform evidence, DCGM for supported GPU telemetry, OpenTelemetry for application journeys, and suitable SPL/PromQL queries for stored evidence.
concepts.mistake: Do not assume one interface exposes every layer or that simulation completion certifies production readiness.

frames.narration: Each course addresses a different layer.
Use identifiers to connect the layers.
Check what is actually supported and observed.
Build an evidence-backed account of the outcome.

check.prompt: What is the appropriate meaning of a course badge?
options: A milestone for the defined learning objectives
check.explanation: Course completion and unrestricted production qualification are different claims.

lab.goal: Build a two-branch incident plan: reduce batch and verify memory for the memory case; inspect cooling and verify clocks for the thermal case. Preserve the original evidence.
hints: Read each scenario before selecting a response.
Choose the layer-specific memory and cooling responses; preserve evidence and inspect the after-state.

questions.prompt: Should memory pressure and thermal pressure always use the same response?
options: No; choose a response supported by the affected constraint
questions.explanation: Different conditions require different evidence and interventions.

questions.prompt: What should accompany a claimed improvement?
questions.explanation: A claim needs an outcome measurement and honest boundaries.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate meaning of a course badge?
options: A milestone for the defined learning objectives
questions.explanation: Course completion and unrestricted production qualification are different claims.

questions.prompt: Why retain the original replay in the incident report?
options: To support diagnosis and a comparable before/after account
questions.explanation: A report needs evidence of what changed and why.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible next step after this hardware-free course?
options: Read compatible real telemetry and validate a small workload with documented procedures
Assume every simulation threshold is universal
questions.explanation: Transfer requires real support checks and workload measurements.

glossary.CPU: General-purpose processor executing control and computation.
glossary.GPU: Device providing parallel processing capability for suitable supported workloads.
glossary.parallelism: Independent or partitioned work performed concurrently.
glossary.workload: Task and data processed by an application.
glossary.kernel: Code launched to perform an operation on a GPU.
glossary.driver: Software enabling supported operating-system interaction with a device.
glossary.runtime: Software managing an application's execution environment.
glossary.input pipeline: Stages delivering prepared input to the computation.
glossary.Redfish: Supported platform-management interface, distinct from complete workload telemetry.
glossary.DCGM: NVIDIA tools and interfaces for supported GPU environments.
glossary.utilization: A field-defined activity measurement over an observation window.
glossary.VRAM: GPU-associated memory with its own placement and capacity behavior.
glossary.host RAM: Working memory on the host system, distinct from ordinary device allocations.
glossary.allocation: Memory or resources assigned to data or work.
glossary.parameter: Stored model value contributing to its computation.
glossary.FP32: Floating-point representation commonly using four bytes per stored value.
glossary.FP16: Floating-point representation commonly using two bytes per stored value.
glossary.INT8: An eight-bit integer representation, with quantization metadata and constraints where applicable.
glossary.precision: Representation choice affecting storage, numerical behavior, and support.
glossary.inference: Using a model to compute outputs from inputs.
glossary.activation: Intermediate computation state, whose memory depends on execution.
glossary.KV cache: Key-value attention state retained in applicable model workloads.
glossary.overhead: Explicit allowance for additional runtime or workload memory in this estimate.
glossary.batch: A group of inputs processed together.
glossary.throughput: Completed useful work per time interval.
glossary.latency: Elapsed time for a defined operation.
glossary.training: Updating model parameters using data and an optimization method.
glossary.gradient: Computed change information used during training.
glossary.optimizer: Method and associated state used to update parameters.
glossary.exporter: Component exposing selected telemetry for collection.
glossary.telemetry: Observed signals about hardware or software behavior.
glossary.label: A dimension identifying a metric's observed resource or context.
glossary.sample: One numerical observation with identity and timing.
glossary.evidence: Observations supporting or challenging a conclusion.
glossary.outcome: Useful application result, separate from hardware activity.
glossary.bottleneck: A limiting stage under a specified workload and objective.
glossary.counter: Cumulative additions whose reset and export semantics must be understood.
glossary.rate: Change per time interval for a suitable quantity.
glossary.energy: Accumulated consumption, such as joules or watt-hours.
glossary.power limit: Supported hardware-specific constraint on power behavior.
glossary.temperature: Thermal reading whose location and equipment limits matter.
glossary.clock: Operating frequency of a device component.
glossary.MHz: Millions of cycles per second, a frequency unit.
glossary.throttling: Reduced operating behavior under a limiting condition; evidence and definitions matter.
glossary.cooling: Physical removal of heat through supported equipment and environment.
glossary.verification: Evidence checking the intended outcome after a response.
glossary.XID: NVIDIA error-identifier vocabulary, requiring documented interpretation and context.
glossary.gauge: A current observation that can rise, fall, or hold an identifier.
glossary.error identifier: Code describing an error class, not inherently an event count.
glossary.ECC: Error-correcting-code mechanisms on supported memory configurations.
glossary.health: Reported condition under defined hardware and telemetry semantics.
glossary.isolation: Restricting use of a suspected resource according to an appropriate procedure.
glossary.maintenance: Planned equipment intervention requiring its own operational procedure.
glossary.data parallelism: Processing different data across computation replicas.
glossary.replica: Repeated instance of relevant model or workload state.
glossary.placement: Assignment of computation and data to devices.
glossary.model parallelism: Partitioning model state or computation across devices.
glossary.shard: Partition of data or model state.
glossary.tensor parallelism: Partitioning applicable tensor operations across devices with framework support.
glossary.pipeline parallelism: Dividing applicable computation stages across devices.
glossary.PCIe: A hardware communication interconnect with topology and bandwidth constraints.
glossary.NVLink: Supported NVIDIA device-interconnect arrangements, dependent on hardware topology.
glossary.collective: Communication or synchronization operation across participants.
glossary.topology: Actual arrangement of devices and communication paths.
glossary.Kubernetes: System orchestrating container workloads with resource and policy constraints.
glossary.Pod: Kubernetes unit grouping containers scheduled together.
glossary.scheduler: Component or teaching model assigning work to eligible resources.
glossary.Pending: Work not yet assigned or running; investigate the actual status and constraints.
glossary.extended resource: Named resource such as a supported whole-GPU resource.
glossary.limit: Declared resource limit under its allocation semantics.
glossary.YAML: Indented text configuration containing objects, lists, and values.
glossary.MIG: Supported Multi-Instance GPU hardware partitioning with defined profiles.
glossary.profile: Supported instance configuration with defined resource characteristics.
glossary.device plugin: Integration advertising supported device resources to Kubernetes.
glossary.Prometheus: Monitoring system collecting and querying time-series observations.
glossary.exposition: Text or protocol representation of samples exposed by an endpoint.
glossary.scrape: Collection of a current endpoint's samples.
glossary.time series: Observations of the same metric identity over time.
glossary.alert: A defined condition requiring an appropriate investigation or response.
glossary.memory pressure: Workload memory nearing or exceeding a relevant budget.
glossary.thermal pressure: A modeled or measured thermal constraint requiring equipment-specific interpretation.
glossary.baseline: Comparable initial evidence before a change.
